clue.text: Gentleman recalled favourite cover of taboo Italian folk song

indicators.note: called back, so the word is read backwards
a cover is the outside, so take the first and last letters

blocks.note: SIR, a title for a gentleman, reversed
a pet is a favourite, as in teacher's pet
the outside letters of TabOO

explanation.surface: A gentleman remembers his beloved cover version of a forbidden Italian folk song.
explanation.walkthrough: "Cover" in the surface is a musician's cover version; here it only means the outer letters. The answer is obscure, so the wordplay has to be trusted.
explanation.definitionFit: A rispetto is a short Italian folk poem or song, usually of love, in eight lines.

clue.text: Little devil, one obtaining exemption from punishment

blocks.note: an imp is a small devil
unity is the number one

explanation.surface: A little devil is the one child who always gets away without being punished.
explanation.walkthrough: "One" usually gives I or A; here it is the whole word UNITY.
explanation.definitionFit: To act with impunity is to act without any risk of punishment.

clue.text: Freshwater fish edges either side of river birds

indicators.note: the edges of a word are its first and last letters
the two letters sit on each side of R

blocks.note: the perch is a river and lake fish
the first and last letters of EdgeS
R = river, as on maps

explanation.surface: A description of where freshwater fish swim and what lives along the riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: "Edges" reads as the riverbanks; it is its own fodder, giving E and S, which then wrap round R.
explanation.definitionFit: Perchers are birds that perch, the group that includes the songbirds.

clue.text: Did appropriate introductions to Treasury obtain approval?

indicators.note: the introduction to a word is its first letter

blocks.note: first letters of Treasury and Obtain
an OK is an approval

explanation.surface: A question about whether the right introductions were made for a Treasury sign-off.
explanation.walkthrough: "Did appropriate" reads as "was it proper"; appropriate is the verb, to take for oneself, so "did appropriate" means took.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: to appropriate is to seize for your own use.

clue.text: Hostile verbal animosity when it’s usually calm?

definitions.note: an adjective phrase describing a quiet time, rather than a noun

indicators.note: spoken, so the word is heard rather than spelt

blocks.note: someone off with you is unfriendly
pique is resentment; said, it matches PEAK

explanation.surface: Someone snapping angrily at a time when things are normally peaceful.
explanation.walkthrough: "Off" meaning cold or unfriendly is British usage ("she was a bit off with me"). The question mark flags a definition by example: off-peak hours are the quiet ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Off-peak times are when trains, roads and phone lines are least busy.

clue.text: Complaint made by others about revised rota

indicators.note: turned about, so the letters are rearranged
changed, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: OTHERS rearranged
ROTA rearranged

explanation.surface: A grievance raised by colleagues about the changed work rota.
explanation.walkthrough: "Complaint" suggests a grumble about the rota; it is an ailment. Each half is scrambled on its own and the two results are joined.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint can be a minor illness, and a sore throat is a common one.

clue.text: Fish eating seaweed that’s hypothetically perfect?

definitions.note: describes the thing rather than naming it; read as "something that's hypothetically perfect"

indicators.note: the fish takes the seaweed inside it

blocks.note: the ide is a European freshwater fish; plural here
an alga, as seaweed is

explanation.surface: A fish eating seaweed and so achieving a notionally perfect diet.
explanation.walkthrough: The fish is plural so that its last letter can close the answer. In physics an ideal gas is a theoretical model that no real gas quite matches.
explanation.definitionFit: An ideal gas is the physicist's hypothetical gas whose molecules behave perfectly by the gas laws.

clue.text: Tip from informer stopping criminal that’s out of line

indicators.note: the informer plugs the gap inside the other word
read literally, the word is left without its line, so L (line) is removed

blocks.note: to rat on someone is to inform on them
GUILTY, criminal, without its L (line)

explanation.surface: A tip-off from a police informer that stops a criminal getting out of hand.
explanation.walkthrough: "Tip" reads as a tip-off from the informer; it is the money left for a waiter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the money left for a waiter or driver on top of the bill, the formal word for it.

clue.text: Fish / move with difficulty

blocks.note: a flatfish of coastal waters
a verb: to struggle or stagger clumsily, as through mud

explanation.walkthrough: Two unrelated meanings of the same word, one a noun and one a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A flounder is a flatfish, and to flounder is to stagger or struggle along.

clue.text: Kindle hits back — book’s ending no longer available

indicators.note: hitting back returns the blows, so the word comes back to front
the last letter of the word

blocks.note: RAPS, hits, reversed
last letter of booK
a dish that is off the menu is no longer available

explanation.surface: A Kindle e-reader proving a hit, while the printed book is out of stock.
explanation.walkthrough: Kindle looks like the Amazon e-reader, capital K and all; it is the verb, to set alight. The capital comes free at the start of a clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To spark off something is to kindle it, to set it going.

clue.text: Data visualisation, mine involving exceptional reach

indicators.note: the mine takes the other letters inside it
out of the ordinary, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: a pit is a coal mine
REACH rearranged

explanation.surface: A chart showing how far a mining operation extends.
explanation.walkthrough: "Data visualisation" and "mine" pull toward data mining; the mine here is a coal pit.
explanation.definitionFit: A pie chart presents data as slices of a circle.

clue.text: Grotesquely morph image copy

indicators.note: distorted, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: Instructions to distort a picture with photo-editing software and duplicate it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is image software; the answer is an old stencil duplicating machine, used here as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To mimeograph a document is to copy it on a stencil duplicator.

clue.text: Is gendarme worried, as Vichy France may have been?

definitions.text: as Vichy France may have been?
definitions.note: describes a past participle by example; GERMANISED is the adjective

indicators.note: agitated, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: Asking whether a French policeman was anxious during the wartime occupation.
explanation.walkthrough: Vichy France was the collaborating regime under German control in the Second World War; the question mark marks the definition as a speculative example.
explanation.definitionFit: Under German domination the Vichy state could be said to have been Germanised, made German in character.

clue.text: Fruit from Italian region peeled

indicators.note: the skin, the outer letters, comes off

blocks.note: pUGLIa, Puglia, without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Produce grown in a southern Italian region, with its skin taken off.
explanation.walkthrough: Puglia (Apulia) is the heel of Italy. "Peeled" suits the fruit in the surface but works on the region's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The ugli is a Jamaican citrus fruit, a cross of grapefruit and tangerine.

clue.text: I got picked up — not a pretty sight

indicators.note: caught by the ear, so the words are heard

blocks.note: got in the sense of understood, as in "I see"; in a non-rhotic accent the phrase is heard as a single word

explanation.surface: Someone collected from the station who admits they looked a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: Got is taken in the sense of understood, as in "I see". The sound match relies on a British accent where "sore" and "saw" rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyesore is something ugly to look at.

clue.text: They get free case of Soave over and above pickled cooking ingredients

indicators.note: the case is the outside, first and last letters
turned over, read backwards
in a down answer, placed on top of the next part

blocks.note: SoavE's outer letters, SE, turned over
capers are pickled flower buds

explanation.surface: Diners who are given a free case of Soave wine along with their pickled capers.
explanation.walkthrough: "Get free" looks like receiving something for nothing; it means breaking out. "And" is part of the placing instruction "over and above".
explanation.definitionFit: Escapers are people who get free, break out.

clue.text: Surviving extremely unusual punches, jubilant in victory

indicators.note: take the extremes, the first and last letters
strikes into, so the letters go inside

blocks.note: extant means still existing
first and last letters of UnusuaL

explanation.surface: A boxer who survived some unusual punches and is jubilant after winning.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a boxing match; "punches" is the instruction to insert UL into EXTANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Exultant means triumphantly joyful, as after a victory.

clue.text: Retreat in theory periodically affords virtue

indicators.note: one part goes inside the other
at regular periods, every other letter

blocks.note: a nest is a snug retreat
every other letter of tHeOrY

explanation.surface: A philosophical claim that retreating, in theory, can be a virtue.
explanation.walkthrough: "In theory" looks like a phrase; "in" is the container instruction and "theory" is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: honesty is one of the classic moral virtues, so the general word stands for it.

clue.text: Wiped out by joke penned by eg top journo

indicators.note: shut inside the next word, like an animal in a pen

blocks.note: X as in 3 × 4, three by four
a pun is a joke
used as is, split round X PUN
the editor, the top journalist

explanation.surface: A top journalist's joke cut from the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The first "by" is not a link word: it gives X, the multiplication sign. "Journo" is informal British for journalist.
explanation.definitionFit: To expunge is to wipe out or erase.

clue.text: Pathetic ragged child got back clothes after having run away

indicators.note: got back is got in return, so the word is returned back to front
dresses, so the word goes round the other
R for run leaves the word

blocks.note: GOT reversed
URCHIN, a ragged child, without R (run)

explanation.surface: A pitiful waif who got some clothes back after running away from home.
explanation.walkthrough: "Clothes" is a verb here, and TOG (as in togs) fits it well. R = run is the cricket abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathetic in its old sense is moving, stirring pity, which is what touching means.

clue.text: Somebody quiet bores intolerant individual

indicators.note: drills into, so the letters go inside

blocks.note: sh! is a call for quiet
a bigot is intolerant

explanation.surface: A quiet person who finds a narrow-minded one tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: "Bores" reads as "is tedious to"; it means drills into. "Somebody" is the noun, an important person.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the noun sense: "he's a somebody" means a person who matters.

clue.text: Cross, Times pursues copper stifling resistance

indicators.note: a pursuer runs behind its quarry, so Times comes after the rest
smothering, so round the other letter

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
R for resistance in physics
the multiplication sign

explanation.surface: An angry Times policeman choking off resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: "Cross" looks like angry; crux is Latin for cross. "Copper" looks like a policeman.
explanation.definitionFit: Crux is Latin for a cross, and the word is still used for a cross in heraldry and astronomy (the Southern Cross).

clue.text: Philosopher from Prussia upset about a load of rubbish

indicators.note: knocked over, so the letters are rearranged
goes around the next part

blocks.note: PRUSSIA rearranged
a tip is a rubbish dump

explanation.surface: A philosopher from Prussia annoyed by some nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: Prussia suggests a German thinker like Kant; Aristippus was Greek, founder of the Cyrenaic school. In Britain a tip is a rubbish dump.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristippus of Cyrene was a pupil of Socrates who taught that pleasure is the highest good.

clue.text: Plants in pretty urn, lilacs, at regular intervals

indicators.note: letters taken at evenly spaced gaps, here every second one

blocks.note: odd letters of PrEtTyUrNlIlAcS

explanation.surface: Flowers arranged in a pretty urn, with lilacs spaced among them.
explanation.walkthrough: "At" belongs to the indicator; the letters run out exactly at the S of lilacs.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain category for example: the petunia is a trumpet-flowered bedding plant, a relative of tobacco.

clue.text: Top-level racing judge, one in a state

blocks.note: F1, Formula One, with the 1 read as I
J = judge, as in legal citations
I = one, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A leading racing judge, one of those in a state of excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: F1 gives FI because the digit 1 and letter I look alike, a common trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiji is an island state in the South Pacific.

clue.text: What may help to keep beehive upright?

definitions.text: What may help to keep beehive upright?

blocks.note: the surface wants a prop or stake, something to steady a structure
a beehive is also a tall piled-up 1960s hairstyle, which needs pinning to stay up

explanation.surface: A beekeeper's question about propping up a hive.
explanation.walkthrough: The beehive is the 1960s towering hairdo, held up with pins and grips, not a bee's home. A hairgrip is the British name for a bobby pin.
explanation.definitionFit: Hairgrips hold a piled-up hairstyle such as a beehive in place.

clue.text: Managed US pop goddess, old hand in Mexico

blocks.note: ran a business = managed it
Cher, the American singer
O = old, as in OT for Old Testament

explanation.surface: Someone who managed an American pop diva and was an old hand at touring Mexico.
explanation.walkthrough: "Old hand" reads as a phrase meaning veteran; "old" is the O and "hand" is a farmhand.
explanation.definitionFit: A ranchero is a ranch worker or rancher in Mexico or the US Southwest.

clue.text: Over-60s righted a wrong

indicators.note: put wrongly, so the letters are rearranged
